newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ monetary conditions seen easier - RBNZ survey.
newsitem.headline: NZ monetary conditions seen easier - RBNZ survey.

text.p: Monetary conditions in New Zealand are perceived to have loosened since February, according to the Reserve Bank's May survey of expectations published on Wednesday.
A net 19 percent of the 241 people surveyed believed conditions were tighter than neutral. That compares with 54 percent in the last survey in February.

Further easing is anticipated with only 3.1 percent expecting conditions to be tighter than neutral by the end of September. Then, by the end of March 1998, the easing is picked to reverse with a net 25 percent predicting tighter than neutral conditions.

Expectations for core inflation have come down, with March 1998 year underlying inflation picked at 1.5 percent and 1.8 percent a year later. One- and two-year-ahead inflation expectations in the February survey were 1.7 and 1.8 percent respectively.
One-year-ahead labour cost expectations have fallen. The labour cost index is now seen rising by 2.3 percent in the March year 1998 year, from a year-ahead expectation of 2.5 percent in February.
GDP growth expectations have eased slightly with year-ahead growth seen at 2.2 percent from 2.4 percent previously.
Ninety-day bank bills are seen at 7.0 percent in June 1997 and to rise to 7.4 percent by March 1998.

Ten year bond yields are picked at 7.7 percent by the end of March, implying an expected positive yield gap of 0.3 percentage points. The RBNZ said a positive expected yield gap had not been recorded since the November 1994 survey.
The current account deficit for the June 1997 year is expected to be $4.1 billion, compared with expectations of a $3.9 billion March 1997 year deficit picked in the last survey.
The deficit is seen widening to $4.4 billion in the March 1998 year.
Of the 241 surveyed on May 7, 54 percent responded.
